meta.blurb: About seventy-five men loaded twelve tons of pig iron a day each. One man, with a stop-watch and planned rests, loaded more than forty-seven. Frederick W. Taylor's 1911 book started an argument that never ended. Read it and judge.
meta.bible: Frederick W. Taylor: an American mechanical engineer, 1856 to 1915, author of The Principles of Scientific Management, published in 1911; the book is in the public domain and retold here in new words. Key terms: Scientific management; Soldiering (workers deliberately working slowly), Natural soldiering, Systematic soldiering; Rule of thumb; First-class worker; Task idea; Planning department; Stop-watch; Mental revolution. Bethlehem Steel Company: a steelworks in Pennsylvania where Taylor did the pig iron, shovel and ball-bearing studies. Pig iron: heavy iron bars of about ninety pounds. Schmidt: the name Taylor gives to the worker in the pig iron story; the gang had about seventy-five men; they loaded about twelve tons a day each; Schmidt loaded more than forty-seven tons; his pay rose from one dollar fifteen cents to one dollar eighty-five cents. Shovel: the best load is about twenty-one pounds; the yard work fell from four to six hundred men to about one hundred and forty. Frank Gilbreth: a builder who studied the motions of bricklayers. The four principles: a science for each part of the work; scientific selection and training of workers; cooperation with workers; an almost equal division of work and responsibility between managers and workers. President Roosevelt: the President whose call to save the nation's resources Taylor recalls in his introduction. Congress held hearings in 1912 at which Taylor gave evidence. Where the book is ambiguous or disputed the retelling says so: later historians question some of Taylor's figures, and his remark comparing a worker to an ox is insulting by today's standards. Voice and tone: clear, fair and balanced; explains Taylor's claims as his claims and does not endorse or condemn them; no invented quotes or numbers.

B1B2: In nineteen eleven, an American engineer named Frederick Taylor published a book called The Principles of Scientific Management. It would change the way factories, shops and offices were run.
Taylor begins with the President's call to protect the nation's forests, coal and iron. He agrees with this call, but he says there is a bigger kind of waste that people rarely notice.
Taylor says that clumsy or badly planned work leaves nothing behind that we can see or touch. Because of this, people rarely notice how much it costs the whole country.
Taylor wants to show that the best way to manage work is a real science. It should have clear laws and rules, instead of depending on habit and guesswork.
Taylor writes that in the past the man has been first, but in the future the system must be first. Good workers will always matter, but even great workers do better inside a good system.
Taylor is careful to add that good people are still needed in every business. In fact, he says that the first aim of any good system is to develop first-class workers.
In the first chapter, Taylor says that the main aim of management is to secure the greatest prosperity for the employer. It should do the same for every worker who works for him.
Taylor says that true prosperity is not a quick profit. It means developing each worker, and every part of the business, to the highest state of excellence.
Many people in Taylor's day believed that the interests of employers and workers are opposed. He answers that, over the long run, their interests are really the same.
Taylor observes that most workers deliberately work much more slowly than they could. In his time, this habit was known as soldiering.
Natural soldiering is the first kind, and it comes from the normal human wish to take things easy. Taylor says that it is something most people do without thinking.
Systematic soldiering is much more serious, because it is planned. Workers agree among themselves to work slowly, so that the employer never learns what a day's work could be.
The first cause is a fear that is easy to understand. Workers believe that if each person produces more, there will be less work to go round, and some of them will lose their jobs.
Taylor argues that this fear is mistaken, and he gives reasons for thinking so. When goods are made cheaply and quickly, more people can afford to buy them, and so more workers are needed, not fewer.

The second cause of soldiering is poor management on the part of employers. When workers earn more under piece rates, the employer often cuts the rate, so they learn that working harder brings no lasting gain.
The third cause is the use of rules of thumb. Each worker follows his own habits and methods, and many of those methods waste time and effort.
Taylor says that skilled workers know many useful things, but they have never written them down. A manager's duty is to collect this knowledge and turn it into clear rules and tables.
In the second chapter, Taylor describes his work at the Bethlehem Steel Company in Pennsylvania. There, a gang of men carried heavy bars of pig iron and loaded them onto railway cars.
About seventy-five men worked together in the gang that loaded the iron. Each of them loaded about twelve tons of iron a day, and that was the usual amount.
Taylor chose one strong, steady worker and gave him the name Schmidt in his book. He offered him a much higher wage, but on one condition, which was that he must do exactly as he was told.

A man stood beside Schmidt with a stop-watch and told him exactly when to lift and when to rest. For this, Schmidt's pay for the day rose from one dollar and fifteen cents to one dollar and eighty-five.
By the end of the day, Schmidt had loaded more than forty-seven tons of iron, almost four times the usual amount. Taylor says that he finished it without being worn out.
Taylor then trained other men, one at a time, in the same way. He says that each earned about sixty percent more pay, while the company paid less for each ton loaded.
Readers today should know two things about this story. Taylor used a phrase about the right kind of man that many people find insulting, and historians have questioned some of his figures.
At the same steel works, Taylor studied the work of men with shovels. He found that a worker does the most work in a day when each shovelful weighs about twenty-one pounds.
Because coal is light and iron ore is heavy, one shovel could not give the right weight for both. Taylor had many kinds of shovels made, one for each material.
Taylor says the yard gang fell from between four and six hundred men to about one hundred and forty. The men who stayed earned considerably more, and the company saved a large sum each year.
Taylor praises the builder Frank Gilbreth, who studied how bricklayers moved. He cut out the wasted motions, for example by putting the bricks on an adjustable platform so that workers need not bend.

In another example, young women checked tiny steel balls for bicycles, a job which needed sharp eyes and steady attention. Taylor chose those with the quickest reactions, gave them shorter hours and rest breaks, and paid them more.
Each of these examples, in Taylor's view, shows exactly the same thing. If you study a job carefully, you can find one best method, and this is rarely the one that people choose by habit.
Near the end of the second chapter, Taylor gathers everything into four principles. They are the heart of the book, and they are worth taking one at a time.
The first principle is to develop a science for each part of a person's work. This science takes the place of the old rule of thumb.
The second principle is to choose each worker with care, and then to teach and develop him. In the past, workers chose their own jobs and trained themselves as best they could.
The third principle is that managers must co-operate heartily with the workers. Only then can they be sure that all the work is done according to the science that has been developed.

The fourth principle is an almost equal division of work and responsibility between managers and workers. Managers take over all the work for which they are better fitted, such as planning, while the workers do the doing.
To carry out the fourth principle, Taylor proposes a planning department. It prepares careful written instructions for each job before the work starts.
Taylor calls the centre of his method the task idea. Each worker gets a clear job for the day, written instructions and the right tools, and he is paid extra for finishing it.
Taylor claims that workers under his system often earned much higher wages. He gives figures ranging from about thirty percent to one hundred percent more than ordinary pay.
Taylor uses the phrase first-class worker for someone who is well suited to a particular job. A person who is not first-class at one kind of work, he says, may be first-class at another.
Taylor insists that scientific management needs a complete mental revolution. Both the workers and the managers must change how they think about their duties and about each other.
Taylor says that both sides usually quarrel over how to divide the profit. In his view, they should turn their attention to making the profit larger, so that each side receives more.
Taylor warns that scientific management is not any single device. It is not time study, a bonus scheme or a system of cost cards, but a whole way of thinking about work.
Taylor also describes his long study of how metal is cut on a lathe. It lasted more than twenty years, and it helped him find the best tools and speeds for each job.
Taylor believes that his principles are not just for factories. He says they apply equally to the management of homes, farms, churches, universities and government departments.
Taylor's book soon became famous, and it was translated into several languages. Managers in many countries studied it, and for a time the word efficiency was on everyone's lips.
Many workers and their unions disliked the new system. They feared that it would treat people like machines and make them work harder for little reward.

Later writers have pointed out some weaknesses in the system. Taylor was perhaps too sure that there is only one best way for everyone, and he paid too little attention to what workers themselves knew.
Many of Taylor's ideas are still used in workplaces today. Standard procedures, time and motion study, and the habit of measuring work all owe something to him and to the people around him.
A modern reader can keep the best of Taylor's lessons. Study the work, test new methods, share the gains fairly, and listen to the people who do the job every day.
The lasting message of the book is simple, and it applies to any job. Question the way you work, test a better method, and treat the people around you as partners, not as parts of a machine.
C1C2: In nineteen eleven, Frederick Taylor, an American engineer who had worked his way up from the factory floor, published a short book with a very large ambition. Its aim was to show that the work of ordinary people could be studied, measured and improved in much the same way that scientists study the natural world. Whether readers loved it or hated it, they found it very hard to ignore, then and in the years since.

In his introduction, Taylor recalls the President's call to save the country's forests, coal and iron ore from being used up too quickly. He agrees with it, but he points out that the saving of materials is only a beginning and that the larger question is national efficiency. A lost ton of coal can be seen and counted, whereas the waste of a day's work leaves no visible trace.

When a forest is cut down, everyone can see the stumps, but when a worker's effort is wasted by clumsy or ill-directed movements, nothing at all remains to be seen. Taylor argues that this invisible loss is enormous, because it is repeated every day in every workshop across the land. He wants his readers to begin looking for it, and to learn to see what has always been hidden.

The purpose of the book, Taylor explains, is to prove that the best management is a true science, resting on clearly defined laws, rules and principles. Until then, he says, most employers had relied upon habit, custom and personal opinion, and few had ever asked whether there was a better way. He promises that his method will rest on careful observation and not on opinion.

In one of his best-known lines, Taylor says that in the past the man has been first, but in the future the system must be first. He does not mean that great leaders are unimportant, only that no organisation can depend on finding a genius for every post. A well-designed system, he argues, lets ordinary people do extraordinary work, day after day, without depending on luck.

Taylor is careful to add that his words do not mean that great people are no longer needed. On the contrary, he says, the first object of any good system must be to develop first-class workers, each one suited to the work that he or she can do best. The system and the worker, in his picture, are meant to grow together and to make each other stronger.

In his first chapter, Taylor states that the principal object of management should be to secure the maximum prosperity for the employer, together with the maximum prosperity for each employee. He insists that these two aims are not enemies, though many people of his day believed otherwise. The whole book, he says, is an attempt to show how they can be reached at the same time.

By prosperity, Taylor does not mean a quick profit that disappears at the next downturn. He means the lasting development of every worker, and of every branch of the business, to the highest state of excellence, so that the good results are permanent. In his view, an employer who ruins his workers for a short-term gain has cheated himself.

A common belief of Taylor's time was that the interests of the employer and the worker are necessarily opposed, so that whatever one gains the other must lose. Taylor rejects this view completely, and he argues that real prosperity for either side cannot last without prosperity for the other. His book is, among other things, a long argument against permanent conflict at work.

Taylor observes that in almost every trade, workers deliberately hold back, doing far less work than they are able to do. The habit was known as soldiering, and he regards it as the greatest evil with which working people in both England and America are afflicted. Because it is hidden from view, it quietly drains the strength of whole industries without anyone noticing.

Natural soldiering, Taylor says, springs from the common human instinct to take things easy, an instinct that most of us share. Left to himself, a person will usually choose a comfortable pace, unless he has a strong reason to hurry. This kind of slowness, Taylor thinks, is less serious than the second kind, which is planned.

The second kind, which Taylor calls systematic soldiering, is far more serious, for it arises from the workers' deliberate and careful planning. Workers agree among themselves on a comfortable pace and keep to it, so that the employer never discovers how much work a day could really produce. A newcomer who works faster than the others may soon feel the disapproval of the group.

The first cause of systematic soldiering, Taylor reports, is a deep and widespread belief among workers that if each person produces more, there will soon be fewer jobs to share. This fear is easy to understand, for a family can be ruined when work is lost, and few people are willing to risk the livelihood of their neighbours. Taylor, however, believes that this fear rests on a mistake, and he says so quite plainly in his book.

Taylor answers that the belief is mistaken, and he points to history, where cheaper production has usually led to more buying, and in the long run to more employment. When goods can be made quickly and cheaply, he says, more people can afford to purchase them, and the makers must hire more hands to meet the demand. Not every economist, then or now, would accept the argument without some careful qualification of its terms.

The second cause, according to Taylor, lies with employers, whose faulty systems of management teach workers to hold back. Under piece rates, where pay depends on how much is produced, a worker who earned more often saw the rate per piece cut, so that his extra effort bought him nothing in the end. Having learnt this lesson once, workers made sure that they did not repeat it.

The third cause of waste, Taylor says, is the reliance on rules of thumb, which means that each worker follows personal habits and half-remembered traditions instead of tested methods. In any trade, he points out, there are dozens of ways of doing a single task, and only one of them can be the quickest and the best. Left to chance and habit, the best way is rarely found, and the old way simply goes on.

The knowledge of the skilled trades, Taylor notes, has always lived in the heads and hands of the workers themselves, and it has been passed on mostly by watching and copying. His proposal is that management should gather this scattered wisdom, test it, and reduce it to rules, laws and tables that anyone could learn. In this way, a craft that once depended on tradition would come to depend on knowledge that was recorded.

In his second chapter, Taylor leaves theory behind and turns to a real workplace, the Bethlehem Steel Company in Pennsylvania, where he put his methods to the test on a large crew. One of the first tasks he studied was the handling of pig iron, which meant carrying heavy bars, each weighing about ninety pounds, from piles in the yard up a plank and into railway cars. The work was simple to describe, but it was brutally hard to do, day after day, in all weathers.

A gang of about seventy-five men did this work, and on an average day each of them loaded about twelve tons, which was the usual amount at the works. Taylor believed that a good worker could do far more than this if the work were arranged sensibly. He decided to find out by choosing one man and studying him with great care.

From the gang, Taylor chose a strong and steady man, whom he calls Schmidt in the book, and offered him a much higher wage for a day in which he would do exactly as he was told. The man was to lift when he was told to lift, and to sit down and rest when he was told to rest, without arguing about the order. Everything depended, Taylor explained, on following the instructions of the man with the watch to the letter.

A man stood at Schmidt's side with a stop-watch, calling out the moment to pick up a bar, the moment to walk, and the moment to sit down and rest. In exchange, Schmidt's pay for the day was raised from one dollar and fifteen cents to one dollar and eighty-five cents, an increase of about sixty percent. For a man in his position, the offer was a large one, and he took it.

By the end of that first day, Schmidt had loaded more than forty-seven tons of iron into the cars, nearly four times the usual amount, and Taylor reports that he did not seem unusually tired. The extra work, according to the book, came not from forcing a man to hurry but from arranging his lifting and resting in the right order. Whether this claim was entirely fair is something that later readers have debated at some length.

Taylor then taught other workers the same method, one man at a time, choosing those who seemed physically suited to the task. He says that each of them earned about sixty percent more than before, while the cost to the company of loading a single ton fell sharply. For Taylor, this was proof that both sides could gain from the new way of working.

Today's readers should treat this famous story with some care, for it has two difficulties. Taylor wrote that such work suited a slow and stolid man, whom he compared to an ox, a remark that most people now find insulting, and historians have since questioned some of his details. Even so, the story remains the best-known example in his book, and it is still told today.

Elsewhere in the same works, Taylor and his helpers studied the shovel, a humble tool that thousands of labourers used every day. After many tests, they found that a first-class worker could do the most work in a day when each shovelful weighed about twenty-one pounds. A load that was heavier tired him too quickly, and a load that was lighter wasted his strength.

Since a shovelful of light coal weighs far less than a shovelful of heavy iron ore, one kind of shovel could never give the right load for every task. Taylor therefore arranged for many shovels of different sizes to be made and kept in a tool room, so that each worker was handed the one that suited his material. The result was that each shovelful came very near to the ideal weight, whatever the material.

Taylor reports that, in time, the work of the whole yard, which had needed between four and six hundred labourers, could be done by about one hundred and forty. The men who remained were paid considerably more than before, and the company saved a large sum every year. It was a striking claim, though it also meant that hundreds of men were no longer needed in that yard.

Taylor also praises Frank Gilbreth, a builder who studied the movements of bricklayers with the patience of a naturalist watching a bird. Gilbreth removed every unnecessary motion, and among other changes he had the bricks placed on an adjustable platform near the wall, so that the worker no longer had to stoop to the ground for each one. Fewer movements meant less tiredness, and less tiredness meant more bricks laid at the end of the day.

In a third example, young women at the same works inspected small steel balls used in bicycle bearings, a task that demanded sharp eyes and unwavering attention for hours on end. Taylor selected those with the quickest reactions, shortened their working day, introduced regular rest breaks, and raised their pay, and he reports that the quality of the inspection improved. Rest, in his experience, was not a waste of time but a way of keeping the mind clear.

What the examples share, Taylor says, is that careful study could find one best way of doing a task, and that this way was seldom the one that workers chose by habit. The best method turned out to be a matter of observation and measurement, not of opinion or tradition. He hoped that readers would carry this lesson far beyond the steelworks and into every kind of work.

Having shown his examples, Taylor now draws out of them four great principles, and these form the heart of the book. He presents them as the duties that management must take up, in place of the old habit of leaving everything to the workers' own ideas. Each of the four, in his view, changes something that most managers had always taken for granted.

The first principle is that management must develop a science for each element of a person's work, to take the place of the old rule-of-thumb methods. This means observing the job closely, timing each of its parts, and recording what is learnt in clear instructions that others can follow. What was once a matter of guesswork and habit becomes a matter of careful measurement and record.

The second principle is that management must scientifically select each worker and then train, teach and develop him, whereas in the past he was allowed to choose his own work and to train himself as well as he could. A person who is poorly suited to a task will seldom do it well, Taylor argues, however hard he tries. The right match, together with proper training, gives the best result for the worker and the employer alike.

The third principle asks management to co-operate heartily with the workers, so that the work is carried out according to the science that has been developed. It is not enough to write the rules in an office and send them down to the shop, Taylor insists, for the rules will only work if the people who use them understand and accept them. He regards the spirit of this co-operation as being just as important as the rules themselves.

The fourth principle divides the work and the responsibility almost equally between the managers and the workers, with each side doing what it is better fitted to do. In the past, Taylor says, almost all the work and most of the responsibility had been thrown upon the workers, whereas now management would take over the planning, the instructions and the preparation of tools. The shop floor, in this way, would be freed to concentrate upon the work itself and nothing else.

To put the fourth principle into practice, Taylor proposes a planning department, a group of people whose task is to think ahead about the work of the whole shop. They prepare written instructions for each job, specify the tools to be used, and arrange the order in which the tasks are to be done. The worker, in turn, no longer needs to waste time wondering what to do next.

The centre of the system, Taylor says, is the task idea, by which every worker is given a definite amount of work to complete in a day, with written instructions and the right tools. If the task is done in the time allowed, the worker earns a substantial bonus, but if it is not, he does not receive it. The reward, in other words, is made large enough to be worth the effort.

Taylor makes a bold claim, which is that workers who followed the new methods earned far higher wages than their neighbours, often thirty to one hundred percent more. These figures are his own, drawn from the factories he knew, and a careful reader will want to weigh them against other evidence. What cannot be denied is that he made higher pay a central promise of his system.

By a first-class worker, Taylor means someone who is well suited to a particular kind of work and is willing to do it well. A person who would be mediocre at one task, he suggests, may be excellent at another, and the manager's duty is to discover which is which. Good management, in this sense, is the art of fitting people to the work they do best.

Taylor insists that scientific management is not mainly a set of tools but a complete mental revolution, required of the workers and of the managers alike. Each side must change its view of its own duties, of its neighbour's duties, and of the work they share. Without that change in attitude, he says, no system on paper could ever succeed in a real workshop.

Taylor points out that employers and workers had long quarrelled over how to divide the surplus, each side trying to take the largest share. Under the new approach, he says, both would turn their attention to increasing the size of the surplus, until it became so large that there was no need to fight about its division. It is an optimistic picture, and he states it with complete confidence, as though it were beyond doubt.

Taylor is also careful to say what scientific management is not, since he feared that many managers would borrow one part of it and ignore the rest. It is not a stop-watch, a bonus scheme or a new system of accounts, he says, but a philosophy that must change the whole relation between employer and worker. A manager who copies the gadgets without the spirit, he warns, will get little from them.

Another of Taylor's examples comes from the machine shop, where he spent more than twenty years experimenting on the cutting of metal. By comparing different tools, speeds and depths of cut, he and his helpers worked out which combinations did the most work, and they turned the results into tables and rules. It showed, he believed, that even a skilled craft such as a machinist's could be improved by patient measurement.

Taylor is convinced that his principles are not limited to the steelworks, and he declares that they can be applied with equal force to all social activities. These, he lists, include the management of our homes, our farms, the businesses of tradesmen, our churches, our universities and our government departments. Readers today may find this confidence surprising, but it explains why the book spread so widely.

The book was soon translated into several languages, and managers, engineers and government officials in many countries studied it with great interest. For a time, the word efficiency was on everyone's lips, and a whole generation of consultants set out to apply Taylor's methods to every kind of workplace. His name became attached to a system, and in time the system outlived him by many decades.

Not everyone welcomed the system, and many workers and their unions believed that it treated people like machines and pushed them to work harder for little in return. In nineteen twelve, a committee of the United States Congress held hearings on the subject, and Taylor himself gave evidence before it. The debate he started about how much to ask of workers, and how to measure it, has never entirely ended.

Later writers have found much to admire in Taylor, but also some real weaknesses. He may have been too confident that a single best method exists for every task and every person, and he paid too little attention to the knowledge and the feelings of the workers themselves. Still, he turned the study of work into a subject that others were forced to take seriously.

Many of the habits that we take for granted in modern workplaces owe something to Taylor and the people around him. Standard procedures, the study of time and motion, the measurement of output and the profession of management consulting all grew, in part, from this tradition. Taylor himself died in nineteen fifteen, but his questions about waste and effort are asked in every office today.

What should a modern reader take from this old book, now that more than a century has passed since it was written? The most useful lessons are probably the habit of studying work with an open mind, the willingness to test new methods against the old, and the principle that the gains should be shared fairly. These can be joined to a respect for the knowledge of the people who do the work every day, which Taylor himself too often overlooked.

The lasting message of the book is that no job is so ordinary that it cannot be done better, and that the search for a better way is a task for everyone involved. Question your methods, measure what happens when you change them, and choose and train people with care. Above all, remember what Taylor himself said at his best, that the aim is prosperity for the employer and for each person who works.
